articles.title: In the 1950s, Hugo Meyer began buying abandoned Vermont farmland to grow timber; his family has now helped permanently protect more than 18,000 acres from development
articles.summary: US News: Growing up in Hardwick on a dairy farm, woods were a major part of Andrew Meyer's life. He would often spend time camping and hiking around East Long .
articles.body: Growing up in Hardwick on a dairy farm, woods were a major part of Andrew Meyer's life. He would often spend time camping and hiking around East Long Pond and as a kid, he visited logging jobs in the area of the Worcester Range with his grandfather or uncle.A history of sustainable timber managementMeyer said his family’s been managing the woods as a working forest since the 1950s, when his grandfather started purchasing land in the region. Hugo Meyer began buying abandoned farmland after World War II to reforest it for timber. In the decades since, the family has owned and managed thousands of acres in and around the Worcester Range, maintaining the land as a working forest. As pressures on land have increased over recent decades, the family felt conservation offered a way to keep the property together and support continued family ownership and sustainable management.“These forests have been part of our family’s story for generations,” said landowner Andrew Meyer. “Conservation offers a way to keep the land together while continuing the stewardship and sustainable forestry practices that have shaped it over the years. We’re proud to be part of an effort that protects the character of this landscape, supports our continued management of this working forest, and helps ensure that future generations can benefit from the same connection to the land that our family has had.”The conserved land includes extensive and varied forest habitat and wetlands, as well as a mile of undeveloped shoreline along East Long Pond. The property has been actively managed for timber for decades and will remain a working forest under the conservation easement. Forest Legacy easements are specifically designed to prevent fragmentation and development while allowing sustainable forestry to continue.Over the years, E.B. Hyde Corp., Meyer's family-run timber company, worked for more than a decade with several partner organisations to bring more than 18,000 acres under conservation easements. In August 2026, they finalised the last of the three phases of the Worcester Woods project, placing more than 3,400 acres into an easement. The project involves a partnership among the Vermont Department of Forests, Parks and Recreation, the Vermont Land Trust and the Vermont Fish and Wildlife Department, along with other partners. Much of the funding for this project came from the U.S. Forest Service’s Forest Legacy Program. That’s revenue that comes partly from leasing federal offshore oil and gas sites.A vital natural corridorAccording to Kate Sudhoff, a land conservation manager at the Department of Forests, Parks and Recreation, what has been conserved by Meyers' family is an important wildlife corridor, a contiguous tract that animals can use to travel across the landscape. It is home to loons and some rare plants and flowers, and there’s a mile of lake frontage on East Long Pond. Its main ecological value, though, is that it’s an intact northern hardwood forest, an important habitat for wildlife in the state. It’s also a high-priority conservation area for the Vermont Agency of Natural Resources. “This one, we always thought of as the gem,” Sudhoff said.“It requires a very patient landowner,” she said, noting it can take years for everything to be finalised. “They have to be really willing and interested in selling these rights and holding the land. And the landowner’s interest in the land has to align with the program.” Meyer is very patient as a landowner. He said trees take 80 years to grow, and he manages his forests in 20- and 30-year cycles. “You have to think long term because these trees take so long to grow, and the health of the forest is critical to that,” he said.For him, the permanent easement will allow the opportunity to think about the future of the land more easily. He doesn't have to worry about development pressure or policy changes ever. “The understanding that that’s really part of the legacy of what my grandfather had envisioned and set forth over 70 years ago,” he said.Easement purchases are a conservation tool where the land remains in private ownership, but the landowner is bound to the restrictions and agreements that come with the easement. For example, easements involving the Department of Forests, Parks and Recreation require that the area be publicly accessible and open for hunting.Will Duane is the land acquisition coordinator with Vermont Fish & Wildlife. He said that even if the landowner decides to sell the land, the easement remains, and the public rights go along with the property. “We’re paying the landowners,” he said. “They’re keeping the land private, but they’re selling some of those land rights to us to conserve it and to bring the public onto it.”The land can’t be subdivided and developed, and an appraisal process determines the difference in value between what the owners might make from selling and developing the land instead of keeping it in conservation. They’re selling those rights, which cost a little less than $5 million for the final phase of the Worcester Woods project.Vermont Fish & Wildlife also purchased from the Meyer family a 301-acre parcel that will become part of the Buck Lake Wildlife Management Area. That expanded the footprint of the Green Mountain Conservation Camp, a popular and affordable summer camp in the wildlife management area where kids can learn outdoor skills and natural science. “It’s a real win-win-win across the board,” Duane said.Meyer now plans to sustainably log the Worcester Woods for many generations. “This is such a big, important piece of land in our region that so many people enjoy,” he said. “Whether they’re the logger cutting the wood, or the hunter or the hiker, or just knowing there are large parcels of contiguous land around them is what makes this region of Vermont so special. “We’re obligated to recognise that and be in the position to help keep that the way it is, and a lot of people are going to benefit from that.”Beyond Vermont’s borders, scientists and conservation organisations have long recognised Worcester Woods as a critical link for climate resilience and wildlife movement. In 2012, the Staying Connected Initiative highlighted the Worcester Range as the “linchpin” connecting larger forest landscapes across northern New England and southeastern Canada.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Putin brings his 'Flying Kremlin' to India for Brics: What makes the 'Doomsday Plane' different?
articles.summary: International News: Russian President Vladimir Putin touched down in New Delhi on Friday to begin a three-day visit for the BRICS Summit, during which he has held a bilat.
articles.body: Russian President Vladimir Putin touched down in New Delhi on Friday to begin a three-day visit for the BRICS Summit, during which he has held a bilateral meet with Prime Minister Narendra Modi to discuss expanding bilateral trade, investment and energy cooperation. As one of the world's most heavily protected leaders, Putin arrived with a high-level delegation and under characteristically tight security, flying in one of two identical Ilyushin IL-96-300PU aircraft, with both jets airborne simultaneously so no one, barring his closest security detail, knows which one he's actually on. This double-decoy tactic isn't new for Moscow, and Putin has used it on previous foreign visits as well.'Aurus' of the skiesThe aircraft itself, often nicknamed the "Flying Kremlin" or the "Doomsday Plane," is a highly customised, specially modified version of the Ilyushin IL-96-300PU, developed by the Ilyushin Design Bureau back in the 1980s. It belongs to an unofficial category of aircraft designed to function as an airborne command post in the event of nuclear war, large-scale disaster, or any conflict threatening critical military and government infrastructure, a category so specialised that only the United States and Russia are known to have built and operate this category of modified aircraft.Powered by four Aviadvigatel PS-90A turbofan engines, the plane can fly roughly 11,000 kilometres without refuelling, and functions as a fully mobile command centre during national emergencies, complete with encrypted satellite communications capable of securely reaching Russia's military, intelligence and government networks from virtually anywhere in the world. It also carries radar-jamming technology and advanced defensive systems, alongside protected radio and data channels built for uninterrupted communication under worst-case conditions. Beyond the security architecture, the aircraft is also fitted out for comfort, featuring a private presidential suite with bedrooms, bathrooms, a kitchen, dining areas and a boardroom-style conference room.Trump's 'beast' of the skiesThe US operates comparable aircraft of its own. The Boeing E-4, codenamed "Nightwatch," was modified from a 747-200B under the National Emergency Airborne Command Post programme and serves as a survivable command post for the President, the Secretary of Defense and their successors. Separately, the Boeing E-6 Mercury, built on the 707-320 airframe, has served since 1989 as an airborne relay linking the National Command Authority to ballistic missile submarines under the Take Charge And Move Out (TACAMO) mission, with the upgraded E-6B variant, fielded in 1998, also capable of remotely controlling Minuteman intercontinental ballistic missiles.

articles.title: A San Francisco house worth about $4.4 million changed hands through 8 disputed deeds in little over a year; the city has now sued to cancel them all and restore the property record
articles.summary: US News: San Francisco legal authorities have filed a lawsuit seeking to cancel eight disputed deeds tied to a $4.4 million house in the exclusive Sea Cliff ne.
articles.body: San Francisco legal authorities have filed a lawsuit seeking to cancel eight disputed deeds tied to a $4.4 million house in the exclusive Sea Cliff neighbourhood, after officials described the case as an elaborate attempt to take control of the property. San Francisco City Attorney David Chiu filed the case in state court, seeking to clear the city's property records and restore the title to its rightful owner. The legal action follows more than a year of disputed quitclaim deeds, questionable ownership transfers and claims by people who allegedly had no legal right to the house. The property sits in one of San Francisco's wealthiest neighbourhoods, overlooking the Pacific Ocean. The dispute grew after neighbours reported that people had entered the vacant house, changed its locks and used disputed documents to claim ownership. According to court filings detailed by The San Francisco Standard, the trouble began after the long-term registered owner, who lives abroad, left the property empty. People then allegedly took advantage of the vacant house by filing a series of documents that created a false trail of ownership in public records. Eight disputed deeds were recorded in connection with the property over slightly more than a year. The city alleges that the documents included false signatures, fake entities and fraudulent notarisation.Public records filled with disputed transfersThe City Attorney's Office says the repeated filings created a serious problem for San Francisco's property records. A fraudulent grant deed or quitclaim deed can place a false ownership history into official records. Even when a document is later challenged, it can create confusion for property owners, buyers, lenders and title companies trying to establish who legally owns a house. That problem became especially difficult in the Sea Cliff case because people occupying the property were able to point to recorded documents when police arrived. Neighbours reported repeated police visits to the house. During some encounters, occupants reportedly produced deeds or other paperwork and argued that they were lawful owners or tenants involved in a private property dispute. Police officers responding to such calls cannot immediately determine whether a deed filed with the county recorder is genuine or whether a signature or notarisation has been forged. That can make it difficult for officers to remove people from a property without a court order. The disputed paperwork therefore helped the occupants maintain their claim while the ownership issue remained unresolved.Neighbours sought help as problems grewResidents living near the property pushed city authorities to intervene after months of complaints about the house and the people using it. Neighbours reported overgrown vegetation, poor maintenance and people coming and going from the property. The vacant home had become a source of concern in the neighbourhood, particularly because its registered owner lives overseas and was difficult for residents to contact. The situation also created security concerns for people living nearby. Repeated calls to police and other city agencies did not immediately settle the dispute because the occupants continued to rely on property documents recorded with the city. The San Francisco Standard reported that neighbours had raised concerns about the condition of the property and the activity around it before the city attorney's office took legal action. City attorneys are now asking a court to decide the validity of the disputed documents rather than leaving the issue to be resolved through individual police calls or private disputes. Under California law, city attorneys can take legal action involving public nuisances and seek court orders concerning documents that are alleged to have been fraudulently recorded. The city's lawsuit asks the court to declare all eight disputed deeds void from the beginning. If the court agrees, the order would allow the San Francisco County Recorder's Office to correct the public record and remove the fraudulent transfers from the property's ownership history. The city is also seeking civil penalties against those responsible for preparing and recording the disputed documents, citing California laws against recording forged instruments.Deed fraud is a wider problemThe Sea Cliff case is part of a broader problem involving property and deed fraud in the United States. Such schemes can target vacant houses, properties belonging to people who live outside the area, estates going through probate and other homes that may receive little day-to-day attention from their legitimate owners. A common method involves filing a forged quitclaim or grant deed that appears to transfer ownership to another person. Once the document is recorded, the person behind the scheme can use the public record to support a claim to the property. County recorder offices generally record documents that meet basic filing requirements rather than determining whether every ownership claim is genuine. That means a fraudulent document can enter the public record before the legitimate owner discovers what has happened. The problem can become more complicated when someone physically occupies the property. Police officers responding to a complaint may see an official-looking deed and have limited ability to determine its validity at the scene.California moves to strengthen owner alertsCalifornia has also taken steps to give property owners earlier warning when documents affecting their homes are recorded. Lawmakers recently approved legislation requiring county recorders to notify property owners when deeds and other property transfer documents are filed against their parcels. The measure is intended to give owners a chance to challenge suspicious filings before a fraudulent transfer becomes more difficult to unwind. San Francisco's case could now put that issue under greater focus. The city attorney's lawsuit seeks a clear court ruling that the eight disputed deeds have no legal effect. A ruling in the city's favour would clear the contested transfers from the property's record and restore the ownership history to the last legitimate title holder. For neighbours around the Sea Cliff house, the case also represents an attempt to end a dispute that has already brought repeated police calls and concerns over the condition and security of the property. The court will now have to determine whether the eight deeds were valid transfers or fraudulent documents that should never have formed part of the property's official record.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: After Trump, who? JD Vance leads  GOP succession talk; Rubio, DeSantis also draw support
articles.summary: US News: Vice President JD Vance is increasingly being seen as a leading contender to succeed President Donald Trump, but Republican voters and delegates are f.
articles.body: Vice President JD Vance is increasingly being seen as a leading contender to succeed President Donald Trump, but Republican voters and delegates are far from settled on who should carry the party’s banner in 2028.Vance was front and centre at the Republican midterm convention in Dallas, where chants of “JD, JD, JD” and “48, 48, 48” broke out, the latter referring to the next US president. Trump also praised his vice president afterwards, calling him a “very talented guy” who “did a very good job.”The show of support came as Trump and Vance urged Republicans to turn out for the November elections, which will also serve as an early test of the party’s prospects beyond Trump’s presidency.Vance himself avoided directly addressing the 2028 race. When a supporter shouted “JD 48!” during his speech, he smiled before responding: “We gotta take care of business this November and then we’ll worry about what comes next.”Still, his position as a potential frontrunner was evident. Some delegates said Vance was a natural choice because of his current role and close association with Trump’s administration.“I think Vance is being groomed for that position. I mean, that’s why he picked him for VP,” said Anthony Johnston, a Delaware accountant who attended the convention, as quoted by AP. “He’s different than Trump. No one’s Trump. But I like him a lot.”But Vance is not the only name circulating among Republicans. Secretary of State Marco Rubio, Florida Governor Ron DeSantis and Texas Senator Ted Cruz also featured prominently in conversations with delegates, highlighting how open the succession contest remains.Rubio, DeSantis also draw supportRubio has emerged as a particularly strong alternative to Vance among some Republicans. Peggy Stanton, a Houston retiree, said she had long believed Rubio would eventually become president.“He’s so knowledgeable. He totally understands international threats, the threats of communism,” Stanton said. “Every single issue I hear him speak on, he gets it. He has charisma. I just feel like he would be a great president.”DeSantis, who challenged Trump for the Republican nomination in 2024, also retains support. Rochelle Brooks, a Dallas IT manager, said she would back the Florida governor if forced to choose now.“If I had to name somebody at this moment, if I was forced, I would say it’s the governor of Florida, Ron DeSantis,” Brooks said. “What he’s done in Florida is a roadmap for what we need to do in America.”For some Republicans, the choice could ultimately depend on whom Trump endorses. Norma Alruosan, a payroll tax analyst from the Dallas area, said she was torn between Vance and Rubio and would likely follow Trump’s lead.“That’s going to be hard,” she said. Her decision, she added, would likely depend on whom Trump endorses.Others said it was simply too early to make a choice. Stephanie Donofry, from Pennsylvania, said both Vance and Rubio had demonstrated their ability to lead.“They are both proven. They are both capable,” she said. “I couldn’t tell you which one I prefer more.”A wide-open fieldThe range of names being discussed reflects the uncertainty surrounding the Republican succession race. Trump remains the dominant figure in the party, and no candidate has formally entered the 2028 presidential contest.There are also potential dark-horse contenders. Some convention attendees mentioned Texas Representative Brandon Gill, while others backed Kentucky Representative Thomas Massie despite his recent primary defeat. Texas Senator Ted Cruz also received support, including from voters drawn to his Cuban-American background.For Vance, however, his proximity to Trump gives him an obvious advantage. Bill Schneider, a Texas finance professional, said he would favour a Vance-Rubio ticket with Vance at the top.“He’s kind of like spending a little bit more time with Trump, kind of see the inner workings, how he is,” Schneider said. “And I think he also has a very similar personality to Trump in terms of very direct. I think he’s very sharp-witted.”Yet the absence of a clear consensus underscores how early the race is. Republicans are already weighing the candidates who could shape the party after Trump, but for now, Vance, Rubio, DeSantis and others remain in an increasingly crowded field.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Bihar’s Vas Sthal Kray Sahayata scheme: Rs 60,000 aid for landless families; key provisions explained
articles.summary: News News: The Bihar government has a scheme that can provide financial assistance of Rs 60,000 to landless and houseless families for purchasing residential plo.
articles.body: The Bihar government has a scheme that can provide financial assistance of Rs 60,000 to landless and houseless families for purchasing residential plots. The Mukhyamantri Vas Sthal Kray Sahayata Yojana is implemented by the Rural Development Department and is aimed at eligible beneficiaries of the Pradhan Mantri Awas Yojana-Gramin (PMAY-G) who do not have land to build a house.Scheme to help landless familiesUnder the scheme, eligible beneficiaries can receive Rs 60,000 directly into their bank accounts to help purchase residential land. The assistance is meant for families living in villages where government land is not available for allotment for housing.The scheme addresses a key hurdle faced by landless PMAY-G beneficiaries. While rural housing assistance can support construction of a house, families without a residential plot may not be able to use that support. The Bihar scheme provides financial assistance towards acquiring a plot, subject to the availability of suitable land.Who can benefit?The scheme is aimed at PMAY-G beneficiaries who are landless and houseless and live in villages where government land is unavailable for residential allotment. Beneficiaries must have a bank account to receive the assistance through direct benefit transfer.Applicants have to submit the required details and documents through the designated authorities of the Rural Development Department. The eligibility and landless status of applicants are verified before the assistance is released.The Rs 60,000 is financial assistance towards the purchase of a residential plot. It does not mean the government is providing a free residential plot to beneficiaries. The availability, location and price of land will depend on local conditions.The scheme therefore seeks to address the land constraint faced by eligible rural families who otherwise qualify for housing support but do not have a plot on which to build a home.Ready to Make a Smarter Property Decision? articles.title: Delhi 2047: The big plan, the bigger question
articles.summary: India News: By 2047, Delhi could be home to nearly 32 million people, need around 1,600 million gallons of potable water every day, generate nearly 26,000 tonnes .
articles.body: By 2047, Delhi could be home to nearly 32 million people, need around 1,600 million gallons of potable water every day, generate nearly 26,000 tonnes of solid waste daily and require roughly 40 lakh additional homes.Those numbers tell a bigger story than population growth. They point to a city that will need to build more — while somehow using less land, less water and fewer resources, without compromising safety, mobility, liveability or the environment.That is the challenge at the heart of the Master Plan for Delhi 2047 (MPD-2047).The Delhi Development Authority (DDA) unveiled the MPD-2047 at the National Media Centre on August 20, 2026, presenting it as the fourth master plan for the capital, with a perspective extending to 2047. The authority has described the plan as a framework for shaping Delhi’s future growth, with its focus spanning housing, mobility, infrastructure, environmental sustainability and efficient land use.The plan comes after earlier master plans for 1962, 2001 and 2021. DDA’s current master-plan framework includes policies on transit-oriented development, land pooling, redevelopment of ageing neighbourhoods and ecological restoration, placing long-term urban growth alongside infrastructure capacity and sustainability.It envisions a denser, more connected and more transit-oriented Delhi, with large-scale housing, redevelopment of ageing neighbourhoods, stronger public transport, green-blue networks, ecological restoration and new approaches to land and infrastructure planning. It also pushes for compact growth, with development increasingly tied to the capacity of roads, public transport, water, drainage, sewerage and other essential services.But there is a larger question: Can Delhi grow at this scale without repeating the problems that already make the city struggle today?The question becomes harder to ignore when incidents such as the recent Satya Niketan building collapse enter the conversation. The tragedy exposed something the master plan itself acknowledges: planning a city is not enough if building safety, approvals, enforcement and infrastructure do not keep pace with growth.So, what does MPD-2047 promise, and can Delhi actually deliver it?More homes, but still affordable?Housing is perhaps the plan’s biggest promise. MPD-2047 estimates the city’s housing requirement at nearly 40 lakh dwelling units by 2047. The strategy combines affordable housing, rental housing, EWS housing, hostels and dormitories, affordable rental housing complexes and redevelopment of existing areas. The government says around 18 lakh affordable homes could come through transit-oriented development, while redevelopment of existing group and government housing could add around seven lakh dwelling units.Land pooling is another major pillar, with the DDA hoping to unlock large areas of land and potentially facilitate up to 20 lakh homes.This is sensible in a land-constrained city. But “affordable” is not simply a number of units. A home is affordable only if households can afford its purchase or rent, utilities, maintenance and commute.That makes displacement an important question. Redevelopment and densification can raise land values and change neighbourhood economics. The success of the housing strategy will therefore depend not only on how many homes are built, but who can actually continue to live in them.MPD-2047 also brings Delhi’s 357 villages into the larger redevelopment conversation. At a conference organised by the Dilli Dehat Project, speakers argued that the plan treats these villages primarily as areas for “regeneration”, rather than recognising them as historic settlements with distinct social, cultural and ecological assets. They also raised concerns about the protection of village commons such as ponds and grazing land, and the impact of road widening and land pooling on existing communities.Density works — if infrastructure keeps upMPD-2047 moves Delhi towards more compact development. It promotes redevelopment of brownfield areas, mixed-use development and transit-oriented growth, while encouraging higher intensity around mass-transit corridors. The plan also allows buildings of more than 100 floors to be developed as landmark projects in areas with adequate infrastructure.The idea is to support compact growth, reduce urban sprawl and free up more ground-level space for public and green areas. But density is not automatically sustainable.Concentrating growth near Metro and other mass-transit corridors can also make public transport more viable. Sustainability of vertical growth will depend on what surrounds these towers — transport, water, sewage, power, fire safety and open space. Building higher can save land, but only if infrastructure rises with it.Every additional floor brings additional demand for water, sewage, electricity, roads, parking, fire services, schools, healthcare and drainage. MPD-2047 itself takes an infrastructure-led approach: new development is intended to be supported by roads, public transport, water, sewerage, drainage, power and digital connectivity.The real test, therefore, is sequencing.Can infrastructure capacity be demonstrated before density is increased?That may be one of the most important implementation questions for MPD-2047.Water: The uncomfortable arithmeticWater may be the plan’s clearest sustainability test.In 2021, Delhi’s water supply was about 935 MGD, against estimated demand of around 1,380 MGD. By 2047, potable-water demand is projected at approximately 1,600 MGD. The detailed augmentation calculation identifies about 401 MGD of additional supply, taking projected availability from roughly 1,000 MGD to about 1,401 MGD.That leaves an apparent gap of roughly 200 MGD against the 1,600 MGD demand estimate.The figures come from different stages and assumptions within the planning calculations, so they should not be treated as a simple supply-versus-demand failure. But they do highlight a genuine vulnerability: Delhi’s future growth cannot depend on finding water after development has already happened.That leaves an apparent gap of roughly 200 MGD against the 1,600 MGD demand estimate.The figures come from different stages and assumptions within the planning calculations, so they should not be treated as a simple supply-versus-demand failure. But they do highlight a genuine vulnerability: Delhi’s future growth cannot depend on finding water after development has already happened.That leaves an apparent gap of roughly 200 MGD against the 1,600 MGD demand estimate.The figures come from different stages and assumptions within the planning calculations, so they should not be treated as a simple supply-versus-demand failure. But they do highlight a genuine vulnerability: Delhi’s future growth cannot depend on finding water after development has already happened.Water recycling, rainwater harvesting, wastewater treatment, groundwater recharge and demand management therefore need to move from supporting provisions to core infrastructure.As MoHUA secretary D Thara recently told real-estate developers, housing projects need green areas, rainwater harvesting, water recycling and sewage-treatment infrastructure rather than simply buildings and roads.Safety: The cost of building without safeguardsThe Satya Niketan building collapse has put Delhi’s student housing and building-safety systems under scrutiny. A five-storey boys’ paying guest accommodation near Delhi University’s South Campus collapsed in September 2026, killing seven people, including five university students.The wider question is how safely Delhi’s high-density neighbourhoods are being managed. In Rajendra Nagar, severe waterlogging and drainage failures have repeatedly disrupted life, while the deaths of civil-services aspirants in a flooded coaching-centre basement in 2024 exposed serious gaps in building use, drainage and enforcement. Similar concerns have emerged around cramped PGs, narrow lanes and ageing buildings in student hubs.These incidents underline that urban growth is not only about adding housing and infrastructure. As MPD-2047 enables redevelopment and greater density, building permissions, structural safety, drainage, inspections and emergency access will have to keep pace.The real question is not how high Delhi can build, but how safely it can grow.So, can MPD-2047 be sustainable?Yes — the plan has the ingredients for a more sustainable Delhi: compact growth, transit-oriented development, affordable housing, green-blue infrastructure and infrastructure-led planning.But a plan is only a framework. Its success will depend on coordinated implementation, enforcement and infrastructure capacity.The key question is simple: Can Delhi build capacity as fast as it builds density?If yes, MPD-2047 could make Delhi more connected, resilient and resource-efficient. If not, it could simply make today’s problems bigger.The plan sets the direction. Delivery will determine the outcome.Get the latest India News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Couple climbs a San Francisco cliff to watch the sunset; rising tide trapped them with only 4% phone battery left before firefighters pulled them to safety
articles.summary: US News: A couple who climbed a cliff at Battery Cranston in San Francisco’s Presidio on Wednesday (Sep 9) evening to watch the sunset were stranded after dark.
articles.body: A couple who climbed a cliff at Battery Cranston in San Francisco’s Presidio on Wednesday (Sep 9) evening to watch the sunset were stranded after darkness fell. With their mobile phone dying, the couple called 911, and firefighters arrived promptly, pulling both of them to safety, the San Francisco Fire Department (SFFD) said.When a cosy sunset view turned into a rescue operationThe couple’s Wednesday evening began like many romantic San Francisco moments: a hike to a scenic cliff, the promise of golden light over water, the kind of memory people plan for. But timing and tide operate by their own logic, indifferent to human plans. They climbed partway up the cliff to get an unobstructed view as the sun dipped towards the horizon. The climb wasn’t as adventurous in daylight. But then darkness fell.What made the location beautiful during golden hour became disorienting in the dark. The rising tide altered their whole plan. Soon, the couple realised their route back down to the beach, the same way they had arrived, was now underwater. High tide almost erased their way out. They were on a cliff face in the black of night, unable to navigate safely downwards, unable to move forwards. Soon enough, they realised they were stranded.“It got dark, the tide came in, so they were not able to exit through the beach how they came in. So they were basically trapped,” SFFD Capt. Mariano Elias told SFGATE.The stranded couple reached for their phones at 9:21 p.m. and dialled 911.One of them knew about an app called What3words, a location service that assigns three-word codes to every spot on Earth. The app is designed for scenarios exactly like this. This gave the rescuers precise coordinates when verbal descriptions failed. The couple transmitted their three-word location, and firefighters began moving towards Battery Cranston.But when San Francisco Fire Department crews arrived in the area, the rescue looked more complicated than they had assumed. It was dark, and the couple was somewhere on the cliff. What3words had narrowed the search area, but it couldn’t pinpoint two people on a rock face.The rescue team arrivesCaptain Mariano Elias of the SFFD recounted what happened next. The couple’s phone was dying, with only a 4% battery indicator. Their power was nearly gone. If it died, the connection would be severed. Communication would end. The firefighters arrived with lights. The couple saw the beams sweeping across the cliff face. They knew help was there, and so they yelled.“They saw our lights when they were on the phone. Interestingly enough, their cellphone only had 4% power. That kind of worried me when I heard that,” Elias told the outlet.A specialised SFFD rescue team descended the cliff face, moving carefully down the stone with cables and harnesses. The climb took time. The couple had been sitting with rising dread and a phone on life support. The rescue team pulled the couple back to safety.“A cliff rescue response was dispatched, and after using a location app and verbal calls, both were found and hauled up to safety using a rope system. Great work by all SFFD members resulted in the 2 people being back to safety in 1 hour, and nobody was injured,” the San Francisco Fire Department said in a social media post afterwards. “This is what we train for, even into the late night.” They also shared images and videos of the operation afterwards. In one photo, the couple is visible on the cliff’s side, with the Golden Gate Bridge framed in the background.Elias added that the cliff wasn’t ‘straight down’ and instead had a gradual decline, but its angle was still too steep for two people to descend safely in darkness.He also advised San Francisco residents and visitors to be aware of their surroundings, especially near the beach or cliffs.Stay on designated trails. The city is beautiful for a reason, but beauty doesn’t negotiate with tides. “We want people to go out and visit our city, but we want people to be careful and stay on trails,” he told the outlet.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Driver killed after plunging 50 feet from LA overpass in horror crash
articles.summary: Brutality in downtown Los Angeles early Friday morning as a car veered off an overpass and plunged 50 feet to the street below, causing the car to flip and k...
articles.body:
A driver was killed in a downtown Los Angeles crash early Friday morning when his car careened off Upper Grand Avenue and plunged about 50 feet to the street below, where it overturned.

The driver, a black male in his 30s, was the only person in the vehicle, and no other vehicles were involved in the accident.

Video footage from the scene showed the mangled black sedan overturned on its hood with heavy damage to the front of the vehicle, as officials from the Los Angeles Fire Department inspected the car and placed a white sheet over it.

A driver was killed in a brutal downtown Los Angeles crash early Friday morning as a car careened off Upper Grand Avenue and plunged about 50 feet to the street below, where it overturned.

A motorist was driving northbound on Upper Grand Ave around 2:30 a.m. when he veered off the roadway and overturned, the Los Angeles Police Department told The California Post. The car fell around 40 to 50 feet to Lower Grand Avenue.

Officials pronounced the driver, a black male in his 30s, dead at the scene. He was the only person in the vehicle, police said. No other vehicles were involved.

Video footage from the scene showed the car, which appeared to be a black sedan, viciously mangled and overturned on its hood. There was heavy damage to the front of the vehicle.

A witness at the scene described what she heard as the car plummeted to the street below.

"I was at the ATM and I heard something go 'boom,' and I said that sounds like a car that fell down here," the witness said, pointing to the street below. "And look, it was a car that fell down here. That's crazy."

When asked whether she had seen a car fall from Upper Grand Avenue before, she said, "Hell no."

The Los Angeles Fire Department was on the scene and appeared to inspect the car before placing a white sheet on it.

Police are still investigating the crash. It is not known whether the driver was impaired.

articles.title: Twenty-five years after 9/11, the World Trade Center's final office tower is rising; the 55-story, 1,226-foot building will become American Express's global headquarters in 2031
articles.summary: US News: Twenty-five years after the September 11, 2001, terrorist attacks destroyed Lower Manhattan's skyline, construction has begun on the final commercial .
articles.body: Twenty-five years after the September 11, 2001, terrorist attacks destroyed Lower Manhattan's skyline, construction has begun on the final commercial office tower planned for the 16-acre World Trade Center site. The 55-storey, 1,226-foot supertall tower at 200 Greenwich Street, known as 2 World Trade Center, will become the global headquarters of financial services company American Express. The company has agreed to become the building's sole tenant. The nearly two-million-square-foot tower is expected to be fully occupied by 2031. Developed by Silverstein Properties on land owned by the Port Authority of New York and New Jersey, the project brings progress to a part of the site that remained largely at foundation level for nearly 15 years because of planning and financing delays. According to reporting by The New York Post, state filings and announcements from American Express and Silverstein Properties, the tower is the final major commercial building in architect Daniel Libeskind's post-9/11 master plan for the World Trade Center site.Modern design replaces long-delayed foundationBritish architecture firm Foster + Partners designed the tower with a series of stepped and offset sections. The design is intended to protect sunlight reaching the nearby National September 11 Memorial & Museum. The building will include more than an acre of outdoor space spread across landscaped terraces and roof gardens. Its office floors will have flexible layouts and could accommodate as many as 10,000 employees. American Express plans to move its workforce from its current headquarters at 200 Vesey Street in nearby Brookfield Place. The company has operated from that location since 1986 and will remain there until the new tower opens in five years. At the groundbreaking ceremony, Denise Pickett, American Express President of Enterprise Shared Services, spoke about the company's long history in New York. "For American Express, this project is far more than a new headquarters," Pickett said. "It is a reaffirmation of our belief in this city, our commitment to our colleagues, and our enduring connection to the community we have proudly called home for nearly two centuries. Since our founding in 1850, New York has shaped who we are, and in turn, we have sought to contribute to its growth, vitality, and success. Today's groundbreaking marks the next chapter in that shared story." Pickett said the new headquarters would also bring employees together in a workplace designed to encourage creativity and collaboration.Tower expected to deliver billions in economic activityThe construction project is expected to create thousands of jobs and generate billions of dollars in economic activity across New York. An independent fiscal analysis by consulting firm AKRF, released with details of the project, estimates that construction will create more than 2,000 union jobs. It also projects about 3,200 direct and indirect jobs across New York City. The analysis estimates that construction will add $5.9 billion to New York City's economy and $6.3 billion to the wider New York state economy. The new tower is also being planned with a range of energy and environmental features. It will use smart-building systems, fully electric heating and cooling and lower-emission construction materials. The project has been submitted for Leadership in Energy and Environmental Design, or LEED, certification. Lisa Silverstein, Chief Executive Officer of Silverstein Properties, said completing the final commercial tower carries significance beyond the construction project itself. "This is an important milestone for our city, American Express, and Silverstein Properties," Silverstein said during public remarks. "But it also symbolizes triumph, and what can be accomplished in this country following what happened here nearly 25 years ago." In state press releases issued by the Executive Chamber, New York Governor Kathy Hochul praised the project's commitment to union workers and American Express' long-term investment in Lower Manhattan. She described the tower as a symbol of resilience and said it would strengthen the area as a global business centre.World Trade Center reconstruction nears completionWhen 2 World Trade Center is completed, it will fill the last major commercial office gap in the World Trade Center complex. The tower will join One World Trade Center, 3 World Trade Center and 4 World Trade Center, along with the Oculus transportation hub and the Perelman Performing Arts Center. The reconstruction of the site has taken decades. Developer Larry Silverstein leased the former World Trade Center complex just six weeks before the September 11 attacks brought down the original Twin Towers. While several other buildings on the site were completed over the following years, 2 World Trade Center repeatedly stalled. The project faced changes in potential anchor tenants, redesigns involving different architects and difficult conditions in the commercial real estate market. Initial foundation work was completed in 2013. The latest construction activity has brought large tower cranes to Greenwich Street as crews begin work on the structure's steel core. A separate residential development planned for the World Trade Center site is still awaiting completion. Known as 5 World Trade Center, the project is being planned by a joint venture between Silverstein Properties and Brookfield Properties and is expected to include about 1,200 homes. The start of vertical construction at 2 World Trade Center nevertheless marks a major step towards completing the commercial redevelopment of Ground Zero. For American Express, the project will provide a new long-term headquarters at one of the most significant sites in modern New York history. For the World Trade Center campus, it brings the final planned commercial office tower closer to reality, 25 years after the attacks changed the Lower Manhattan skyline.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Russia unveils new S-71K stealth missile for Su-57E amid potential sale to India
articles.summary: News News: Russia has publicly unveiled the S-71K Kovyor, a new air-launched stand-off weapon designed for its Su-57E fifth-generation fighter, during the El Ala.
articles.body: Russia has publicly unveiled the S-71K Kovyor, a new air-launched stand-off weapon designed for its Su-57E fifth-generation fighter, during the El Alamein International Airshow in Egypt. The weapon was displayed alongside the S-71M Monokhrom as Russia showcased a new generation of air-launched systems that combine features of cruise missiles and low-cost attack drones.Russia is presenting the systems as a new class of relatively inexpensive stand-off weapons, aimed at giving its aircraft the ability to strike targets from a distance without relying solely on larger and more expensive cruise missiles.The aircraft was displayed with several air-to-air and air-to-ground weapons at El Alamein, while Russia's state-owned Rostec said the Su-57E would be shown with weapons that had not previously been demonstrated either in Russia or abroad.The S-71 family also reflects a shift in Russia's approach to stand-off warfare. The new weapons are positioned between sophisticated, high-cost missiles and cheaper attack drones, potentially allowing Russian aircraft to employ larger numbers of expendable weapons against targets protected by air-defence systems.The concept has gained importance from Russia's experience in the Ukraine war, where large-scale use of drones and relatively inexpensive precision weapons has become a major feature of air operations.Russia’s unveiling of the S-71K comes as Moscow is intensifying its push to sell the Su-57E to India, with the fighter now explicitly featuring in high-level India-Russia discussions.Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said this week that the sale of Su-57 aircraft to India is on the agenda of President Vladimir Putin’s talks with Prime Minister Narendra Modi. He also confirmed that Moscow and New Delhi are discussing India’s request for access to Su-57 production technology.Moscow has offered joint production of the Su-57 in India, with Russian officials previously saying technical discussions were underway on the possibility of manufacturing the fifth-generation fighter locally.S-71K KovyorS-71K Kovyor is powered by an R500 turbojet and reportedly has a range of around 300 km. The missile carries a 250-kg OFAB-250-270 fragmentation warhead and uses inertial navigation to strike pre-programmed targets. Its flattened, angular airframe is designed to reduce radar visibility.A Russian arms-export representative told Reuters that the S-71K had already been used in combat before its first public display, while Ukrainian intelligence has said it was first deployed in late 2025.Its key significance is the combination of stand-off range, lower cost and reduced observability, allowing the Su-57 to attack defended targets from greater distances while potentially using the weapon in larger numbers.

articles.title: Two days after Norway King Harald's funeral, his sister princess Astrid passes away
articles.summary: Europe News: Princess Astrid of Norway, the elder sister of late King Harald V, died on Friday at the age of 94, the Norwegian royal palace said, just two days aft.
articles.body: Princess Astrid of Norway, the elder sister of late King Harald V, died on Friday at the age of 94, the Norwegian royal palace said, just two days after she attended her brother’s state funeral in Oslo.Astrid’s death comes less than two weeks after Harald died aged 89 on August 28, ending his more than 35-year reign. She made her final public appearance on Wednesday, September 9, when Norway held a state funeral for the late king at Oslo Cathedral.“Throughout her long life, Princess Astrid represented the royal house in a warm and dutiful manner,” King Haakon VIII said in a statement announcing her death.Astrid, who was born in 1930, had continued to represent the Norwegian royal family at official events despite stepping back from many public duties in recent years.King Harald’s funeralHarald’s funeral on Wednesday marked the end of 13 days of national mourning following his death. His coffin was carried in a procession from the Royal Palace to Oslo Cathedral, with members of the Norwegian royal family and visiting dignitaries taking part. A 21-gun salute marked the start of the procession, while thousands of people lined the streets of Oslo to pay their respects.The funeral service at Oslo Cathedral was preceded by a nationwide minute of silence. It was attended by Queen Sonja, Harald’s widow, his son and successor King Haakon VIII, Queen Mette-Marit and other members of the royal family. Royals and leaders from several countries also attended, including Britain’s Prince William, who represented King Charles.Harald was laid to rest at Akershus Fortress following the service. He had become king in 1991 and was widely known for his close connection with the Norwegian public during more than three decades on the throne.Astrid’s appearance at the funeral was therefore her last public engagement. She had stood alongside members of the royal family as Norway bid farewell to the monarch who had been her younger brother and king for more than three decades.No details have yet been announced about Princess Astrid’s funeral.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Palantir cofounder Joe Lonsdale is unhappy with the US government's idea of sending $5,000 checks to Americans; says: I wants Republicans to win mid-terms, but this is ...
articles.summary: Tech News News: Palantir cofounder Joe Lonsdale has come out against US President Donald Trump's proposal to send $5,000 checks to every adult American if Republicans.
articles.body: Palantir cofounder Joe Lonsdale has come out against US President Donald Trump's proposal to send $5,000 checks to every adult American if Republicans keep control of Congress in the November midterm elections. The major Republican donor called the "Trump dividend" a bribe in a post on X, while making it clear he still wants the party to win."For the record, I am hugely in favor of winning the midterms, and love much about this admin, but am strongly against bread and circus bribes," Lonsdale wrote. The post went up around the time The Great American Midterm Party, which he co-hosted with Donald Trump Jr. on the sidelines of the Republican convention in Dallas, was scheduled to be underway.Plantir cofounder mocks Trump's $5,000 dividend with a '5 million USD' replyLonsdale, who endorsed Trump before the 2024 election, followed up with sarcasm. Replying to a user who argued Americans deserved the money, he wrote that 5K was too small. "Why not 5 million USD to everyone?" he asked, adding, "we can just print money, right?"The phrase "bread and circuses" comes from the Roman satirist Juvenal and refers to keeping the public content with free food and entertainment.Trump's $5,000 midterm pledge would cost the US about $1.2 trillionTrump unveiled the plan on Wednesday at the Republican Party's first-ever midterm convention, likening it to a company handing out cash to its shareholders. He said the money must be spent in the US but did not explain how that would be tracked.With roughly 240 million adult citizens, the payout would cost about $1.2 trillion. That is close to eight times the $154.5 billion the US collected in tariffs in the first 10 months of this fiscal year. Vice President JD Vance has pointed to tariff revenue as a funding source and suggested wealthy Americans may not qualify.Trump also claimed in a TV interview that Congress would not need to approve the payments, though tariff revenue can only be spent through legislation. His earlier promises of a $2,000 tariff dividend and a payout from DOGE savings never materialised.Republicans are split over the Trump dividendLonsdale is not the only Republican pushing back. South Carolina Representative Ralph Norman, vice chair of the House Freedom Caucus, cited the country's $40 trillion debt and said he did not know where the money would come from. Former congressman Justin Amash called it a "ridiculous, unrealizable bribe", and former Arkansas governor Asa Hutchinson urged party leaders to vote it down.Others are on board. Ohio Senator Bernie Moreno said he would prepare legislation to pass the dividend immediately, while Texas Senator Ted Cruz described it as a tax rebate. Senate Majority Leader John Thune said it was a "good question" whether the votes would be there.Democrats, including Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, have accused Trump of trying to bribe voters. articles.title: 'Trade barriers rising globally, India building bridges': PM Modi at Brics business forum
articles.summary: India News: Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Friday positioned India as a bridge-builder in an increasingly fragmented global economy, saying the country is respon.
articles.body: Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Friday positioned India as a bridge-builder in an increasingly fragmented global economy, saying the country is responding to rising trade barriers by expanding free-trade partnerships, strengthening supply chains and creating new avenues for businesses across the BRICS grouping.Addressing the Leaders' Session of the BRICS Business Forum in New Delhi, PM Modi said the global trading environment is becoming more difficult as countries increasingly turn to tariffs, restrictions and other barriers to protect domestic industries. Against this backdrop, he said, India is pursuing greater economic integration by negotiating and signing trade agreements with a growing number of countries.“Today, while trade barriers are rising globally, India is building economic bridges. Since 2014, we have entered into free trade agreements with nearly 40 countries,” PM Modi said.The Prime Minister's message was aimed not only at highlighting India's expanding trade network but also at presenting the country as a stable and increasingly attractive destination for investment at a time when global businesses are trying to reduce their dependence on concentrated supply chains.“Our approach remains focused on reducing barriers and expanding opportunities for businesses,” PM Modi said.India seeks deeper economic role within BricsPM Modi also used India's Brics presidency to push for greater economic cooperation among the 11-member grouping.Rather than limiting Brics cooperation to government-to-government engagement, India is seeking to create networks that allow companies, startups and smaller businesses to access new markets, investment and technology.Under India's chairship, new cooperation networks have been established in areas including agriculture, healthcare, skills development and smart grids. These initiatives are intended to translate the political and economic weight of BRICS into practical opportunities for businesses.India has also launched the Brics Incubator Network, Brics MSME Portal and Brics Startup Innovation Fund.These initiatives are particularly significant for startups and micro, small and medium enterprises, which often face greater difficulties than large corporations in entering overseas markets, finding investors and establishing business partnerships.“To connect startups and MSMEs with markets and finance, we have launched initiatives like the Brics Incubator Network, the Brics MSME Portal, and the Brics Startup Innovation Fund,” PM Modi said.He urged businesses from Brics countries to use these platforms to increase the movement of investment, technology and talent across member economies.Supply-chain resilience becomes a key priorityA major theme of PM Modi's address was economic resilience. The disruption of global supply chains in recent years, from the Covid-19 pandemic to geopolitical conflicts and trade tensions, has pushed countries to diversify sources of energy, technology, raw materials and manufactured goods.India, PM Modi said, has been working to make its supply chains more diversified and reliable.“The theme of India's Brics chairmanship is 'Building for Resilience, Innovation, Cooperation, and Sustainability.' Over the past 12 years, India has made this mantra the foundation of its economic and trade policies,” he said.He pointed to India's efforts across sectors ranging from energy to technology, arguing that stronger and more diversified supply chains would help the economy withstand external shocks.“It is a result of this resilience that, even amidst global uncertainties, India today offers the assurance of growth and stability,” the PM said.The emphasis on resilience also reflects India's broader push to reduce vulnerabilities in strategically important sectors. The government has increasingly sought to build domestic manufacturing capacity while simultaneously attracting global companies looking to diversify production beyond existing manufacturing hubs.Infrastructure and strategic technologiesPM Modi highlighted infrastructure expansion as another pillar of India's economic strategy.India is rapidly expanding its network of roads, railways, ports and airports, he said, arguing that better physical connectivity is essential for lowering logistics costs and improving the movement of goods and people.At the same time, the government is trying to build domestic capabilities in technologies and industries that could have long-term economic and strategic importance.“We are rapidly expanding our roads, railways, ports, and airports. Simultaneously, we are building new capabilities in strategic sectors such as shipbuilding, semiconductors, quantum technology, critical minerals, and biotechnology,” PM Modi said.These sectors are increasingly important because they sit at the intersection of economic security and national security.Semiconductors, for example, are essential for everything from smartphones and automobiles to advanced weapons and artificial intelligence systems. Critical minerals are required for batteries, electronics and clean-energy technologies, while shipbuilding is important both for trade and maritime security.By expanding domestic capabilities in such areas, India is seeking to become not merely a large consumer market but a producer and supplier within global value chains.UPI as India's digital infrastructure modelPM Modi also highlighted India's digital public infrastructure, particularly the Unified Payments Interface (UPI), as an example of how technology can expand economic participation.UPI has transformed the way payments are made in India by enabling fast digital transactions between bank accounts and mobile applications. PM Modi said the system has given fresh momentum to financial inclusion and digital payments on a massive scale.“Today, 50% of the world's real-time payments take place using this technology,” he said.India has increasingly sought to promote its digital infrastructure model internationally, particularly among developing economies. The broader objective is to demonstrate how digital systems can bring more people and businesses into the formal economy while making transactions faster and cheaper.Brics seeks greater business-to-business engagementThe Brics Business Forum is the grouping's main private-sector platform, bringing together business leaders, government ministers and heads of state to discuss trade, investment, finance, technology and development.Its importance extends beyond discussions at individual meetings. Recommendations from the Brics Business Council and the Business Forum can feed into summit declarations and subsequent work programmes, giving the business community a role in shaping the bloc's economic agenda.The Leaders' Session in New Delhi was attended by Brics leaders, the Chairs of the Brics Business Council and the Brics Women's Business Alliance. Modi also joined the participating dignitaries for a group photograph.The forum is being held as India hosts the 18th Brics Summit under its 2026 chairship. India's presidency is centred on the theme “Building for Resilience, Innovation, Cooperation and Sustainability”, with development, sustainability and innovation among its principal priorities.Why Brics matters to IndiaBrics has expanded considerably from its original five-member format and now comprises 11 countries: Brazil, China, Egypt, Ethiopia, India, Indonesia, Iran, Russia, Saudi Arabia, South Africa and the UAE.Collectively, the grouping represents around 49.5% of the world's population, 40% of global GDP and 26% of global trade, according to background information on India's 2026 chairship.For India, the economic significance of Brics therefore goes beyond the traditional diplomatic role of the grouping. Its large consumer markets, energy producers, manufacturing economies and emerging technology sectors create opportunities for greater trade and investment.PM Modi's address sought to underline India's position within that changing economic landscape: as a country attempting to keep markets open, diversify supply chains, build strategic industrial capacity and use its digital infrastructure to expand economic participation.His broader pitch was that as geopolitical tensions and protectionism reshape global commerce, India wants to position itself as a reliable economic partner, one that can connect businesses, markets, investment and technology across an increasingly fragmented world.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Outrage in Germany as AfD politician says arms key to deportation push
articles.summary: German politicians responded with outrage on Friday to comments by a leading member of the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) in which he linked a plann...
articles.body:
Ulrich Siegmund of the far-right AfD party in Germany linked a planned deportation drive to the availability of military equipment, sparking outrage among politicians.

The AfD in Saxony-Anhalt has vowed to carry out a major "remigration" drive if it takes control of the state government, despite facing legal hurdles and opposition from mainstream parties.

The populist Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance (BSW) might offer tacit support to an AfD-led minority government, but even BSW officials sharply condemned Siegmund's remarks, stating that deportations are not a military task.

German politicians responded with outrage on Friday to comments by a leading member of the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) in which he linked a planned deportation drive to the availability of military equipment.

Ulrich Siegmund, who is vying to become Germany's first far-right state leader since World War II after his party overwhelmingly won Sunday's election in the eastern region of Saxony-Anhalt, was asked by a journalist on Thursday about plans by Israeli arms company Elbit Systems to set up a production facility in the state.

"We do not demonize the production of military equipment across the board, because we will, of course, need the necessary resources for [our] planned campaign of remigration and deportation," Siegmund responded.

The AfD has vowed to carry out a major "remigration" drive if it manages to take control of the state government in Saxony-Anhalt. The term is widely used in far-right circles to describe large-scale deportations.

Such plans would likely face significant legal hurdles. Germany's 16 federal states have widespread powers in areas including education and security, but migration policy is decided by the national government.

It is also unclear whether the AfD will be able to govern in Saxony-Anhalt, despite garnering nearly 44% in the vote, as all other mainstream parties have ruled out cooperating with the far right.

The party might be able to rely on tacit support from the populist Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance (BSW), which has indicated it might support an AfD-led minority government.

But even BSW officials sharply condemned Siegmund's remarks on Friday.

"Deportations are not a military task," Claudia Wittig, deputy leader of the BSW parliamentary group in the state parliament, told dpa, adding that military equipment could not be used for this purpose.

"Ulrich Siegmund clearly hasn't thought this through," Wittig said, adding that his remarks came across as a provocation and may indicate an insufficient understanding of the legal situation.

articles.title: An Australian SPF50+ sunscreen tested as low as SPF 4; after 20 products were recalled, its formula maker now faces multimillion-dollar lawsuits
articles.summary: Rest of World News: A sunscreen manufacturer whose base formula was used in 20 products recalled in Australia after they failed to meet their advertised SPF claims is fac.
articles.body: A sunscreen manufacturer whose base formula was used in 20 products recalled in Australia after they failed to meet their advertised SPF claims is facing multimillion-dollar legal claims. Wild Child Laboratories is being sued in the Federal Court over allegations of misleading and deceptive conduct.The issue came to light last year after an ABC news Australia investigation and testing by consumer group Choice led to a series of sunscreen recalls. One of the products involved was Ultra Violette’s Lean Screen SPF50+, which Choice testing found had an SPF of just four.Ultra Violette is now seeking millions of dollars from Wild Child Laboratories. The company alleges that Wild Child made several representations that its sunscreen had an SPF of 50 or 50+, but tests it commissioned later returned much lower results.The legal action has become more complicated because Wild Child Laboratories went into voluntary liquidation in August. The company had sold its assets to a newly established business called Heliora about a month earlier. Heliora continued the sunscreen manufacturing business and had the same CEO and director involved.Tests found shocking SPF levelsAccording to Ultra Violette’s statement of claim, the company commissioned SPF testing between July and September 2025. Seven test results from four laboratories returned average SPF ratings of 2.9, 3.0, 3.6, 4.1, 10.5, 21.5 and 25.18.The claim also referred to another test commissioned by Wild Child Laboratories, which returned an SPF result of 21.7.Ultra Violette has accused Wild Child of misleading and deceptive conduct and breach of contract. The company is listed in the liquidator’s creditor report as being owed $7 million.Wild Child has disputed liability. In its defence filed in July, the company argued that Ultra Violette, as the sponsor of the therapeutic product, was responsible for ensuring the sunscreen met its label claim.“Ultra Violette undertook responsibility for meeting all the legal obligations required of a sponsor of therapeutic goods in Australia in relation to the Lean Screen SPF50+ sunscreen,” the defence said, as quoted by ABC.Wild Child also argued that the companies it hired to carry out SPF testing were “concurrent wrongdoers”. One of those companies was Princeton Consumer Research, or PCR, whose SPF testing data had been questioned.20 recalled sunscreens shared the formulaThe Ultra Violette product was among 20 sunscreens made using the same Wild Child base formulation that were recalled after low SPF test results.The Therapeutic Goods Administration said at the time that preliminary testing indicated the base formulation was unlikely to have an SPF higher than 21, while some products could have an SPF as low as four. Wild Child has since discontinued the formula used in the recalled products.Another company taking legal action is Advanced Skin Technology, the owner of Aspect Skincare. It recalled two sunscreens last year and has alleged that Wild Child failed to take reasonable care in developing, manufacturing and supplying the products and in ensuring they were SPF50+.The company is seeking losses including refunds, credits, write-offs, lost sales and profits, staff time spent on the recall and reputational damage. It has not specified the amount of damages it is seeking, although the liquidator’s report lists almost $2.5 million in debts owed to the brand. Wild Child indicated in a defence filed in April that it would defend the action.Wild Child creditors claim about $20 millionThe legal claims come as Wild Child’s liquidation leaves a number of creditors seeking payment. Documents filed as part of the liquidation show that 11 sunscreen companies are claiming more than $19 million in total.The Australian Taxation Office is also owed more than $400,000. Prominent Australian sunscreen brand Naked Sundays is listed in the liquidator’s report as being owed $8.2 million.The liquidation has also raised questions about the transfer of Wild Child’s business to Heliora. Wild Child sold its assets to the new company in the month before entering liquidation. Heliora shared the same CEO and director and continued the manufacturing business.Heliora said it “firmly rejects any suggestion that it was established as a means of avoiding Wild Child’s liabilities”. “The liquidators have not raised concerns with us about the transaction,” the company said.Heliora said the purchase was negotiated with the involvement of a secured lender to Wild Child and a restructuring advisory firm. It also said the new company had assumed agreed liabilities involving many Wild Child suppliers and creditors.“All Wild Child employees were offered employment with Heliora, and their employee entitlements carried forward,” Heliora said.The company has also continued the manufacturing business under Wild Child’s TGA manufacturing licence. Heliora said it had submitted the required documents to the TGA to support the transfer of the Good Manufacturing Practice licence.SPF, or sun protection factor, refers to protection against UVB radiation. According to the Cancer Council information included in the ABC report, SPF20 filters about 95 per cent of UVB rays, while SPF50 filters about 98 per cent.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: MPs vote against fresh attempt to legalise assisted dying
articles.summary: The proposed law sought to introduce one of the biggest societal changes in recent years.
articles.body:
MPs have voted against proposals to legalise assisted dying in England and Wales, bringing the latest effort to change the law to an end.

Following a debate in which both sides made emotional speeches, the House of Commons voted 286 to 270, majority 16, against the proposed legislation.

The Terminally Ill Adults (End of Life) Bill would have allowed adults with fewer than six months to live to apply to be given help to end their own life, subject to certain safeguards.

A similar bill in the last parliamentary session was supported by MPs before stalling in the House of Lords . The decision from MPs on Friday rules out the prospect of changes to the law on assisted dying in the short-term.

The bill tabled by Labour MP Lauren Edwards will make no further progress, although MPs and peers could make another attempt in the next parliamentary session.

Assisted dying is an issue that has been debated for hundreds of hours in Parliament over the last two years and would have represented one of the biggest societal changes in recent years if it had been approved.

MPs were given a free vote, meaning they did not vote on party lines.

Safeguards within the bill included a requirement that a person applying for an assisted death had the approval of two doctors and an expert panel.

But critics said it included too few measures to protect vulnerable people from being coerced into ending their lives, while some say improving palliative care should be the priority.

There were emotional scenes outside Parliament from both sides after MPs voted against giving the bill a second reading.

Dame Esther Rantzen, who was unable to join supporters in Parliament Square, told the BBC that it was "so sad that people in this country won't have the choice" that terminally ill adults have in other countries.

The Childline founder said: "I am sure a change in the law will come. I am deeply sad that it won't come soon enough for many of the people who need it, it's a tragic day."

The broadcaster, 86, is terminally ill with cancer and has said she is now "too physically fragile" to travel to Switzerland to end her life at an assisted suicide clinic.

Edwards, the Labour MP for Rochester and Strood, said: "Parliament has dropped the ball today.

"It will be picked up again as it must be, because the law as it stands is simply too cruel and too unjust to be allowed to stand."

Labour MPs Ashley Dalton, Dame Meg Hillier and Jess Asato, who all opposed what they described the "unsafe and unworkable" bill, welcomed the decision.

In a joint statement, they said: "This is not a moment for celebration, we understand the deep concerns of so many people across the country who have campaigned hard for a change in the law.

"But the truth is none of the relevant royal medical colleges, professional groups or experts will attest to the safety or workability of this bill."

They said there is a need to "fix our NHS and sort out social and palliative care before we even consider introducing assisted dying".

Sarah Wootton, chief executive of Dignity in Dying, said "thousands of terminally ill people will continue to suffer against their wishes in their last days and weeks".

She added she still believes "law change is inevitable".

Care Not Killing chief executive Gordon Macdonald described the vote as "decisive".

He said: "Our hope is that MPs now focus on repairing palliative care in the UK and securing the necessary funding to make sure that no matter what part of the country you live in, you can access the best possible care available and are treated with dignity and respect."

The bill in the last parliamentary session was brought forward by Labour MP Kim Leadbeater and cleared the House of Commons on 20 June 2025 with a majority of 23.

But it ran out of time to progress through all the necessary stages in Parliament after some peers in the House of Lords tabled more than 1,200 amendments.

Edwards brought forward the proposals again in a bid to ensure peers could "finish their job", although this will no longer take place.

During the debate, Labour MP Janet Daby was among those to confirm she would vote against the bill despite previously supporting it.

She told the Commons she had "nightmares about dying and death" after voting in favour of the last bill, adding: "I had to wrestle with myself, knowing that I was not entirely comfortable with the decision I had made, and my conscience was not at peace, and I cannot again, in good conscience, vote for the bill."

In another of the personal testimonies during the debate, Labour MP Claire Hazelgrove spoke about her mother's decision to bring her late-stage terminal illness to an end "on her terms".

The MP for Filton and Bradley Stoke said the "harmful status quo" meant her mother died alone in October last year, after living with a rare blood cancer for half her life.

Hazelgrove argued "not all pain can be palliated" as she spoke in favour of the bill.

Conservative MP Martin Vickers said his "firm" view was that "if assisted dying is legalised we will be poorer as a society, we will have a crossed a line", adding it would also change the "relationship between doctor and patient".

Liberal Democrat MP Tom Gordon called for a change in the law and described the bill as "better than what we currently have, which offers no safeguards and no protections for people in those final moments".

Prime Minister Andy Burnham did not vote on the bill on Friday, previously describing it as "a matter for Parliament to decide".
